newsitem.title: USA: U.S. would back U.N. on delaying Angola sanctions.
newsitem.headline: U.S. would back U.N. on delaying Angola sanctions.

text.p: The United States said on Friday it wanted to tighten sanctions on Angola's UNITA faction but would go along with U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan if he wanted to delay them.
"The United States supports additional sanctions," State Department spokesman James Rubin told reporters.
"However, we're prepared to give the secretary general flexibility if he thinks he needs it," Rubin said.
In a report issued on Friday, Annan said UNITA's compliance with the Angolan peace accords was unsatisfactory.
But diplomats said the U.N. chief wanted any sanctions imposed upon the rebel movement delayed.

They said the Security Council next week might impose sanctions but give a two-week grace period before they went into effect. Or it might postpone any resolution until September while the United Nations verifies new proposals from UNITA.
Rubin called UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi "an unhelpful player in the process in recent months."

"He has not agreed to allow the Angolan government to take control of the necessary parts of Angola that he had control of (and) he has tens of thousands of (armed) troops under his command .... who have not demobilized," Rubin said.
Also Savimbi "has refused to go to the capital and participate in the government the way the Lusaka Protocol requires," the spokesman said.
As a result, "we should be prepared to consider sanctions and we are ready, willing and able to consider a tighter sanctions package on UNITA," he said.

But Rubin added that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's instincts, as former U.N. ambassador, are "to give the benefit of the doubt to the secretary general when it comes to implementing details of an agreement unless there's a really compelling reason not to."
